Respiratory arrest with a pulse

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A 45-year-old man is unresponsive and apneic after a suspected opioid overdose. A definite carotid pulse is present. A trained rescuer begins bag-mask ventilation while another prepares naloxone and reassessment. Which initial adult ventilation pattern is appropriate?

  1. One breath every 6 seconds with visible chest rise
  2. One breath every 2 seconds regardless of chest rise
  3. Thirty compressions before every two breaths despite the definite pulse
  4. One breath every 30 seconds
  5. No ventilation until naloxone takes effect
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

One breath every 6 seconds with visible chest rise

For an adult with a pulse but absent normal breathing, provide approximately 10 breaths per minute and reassess.

Understanding the options

One breath every 6 seconds with visible chest rise
For an adult with a pulse but absent normal breathing, provide approximately 10 breaths per minute and reassess.
One breath every 2 seconds regardless of chest rise
This risks excessive ventilation.
Thirty compressions before every two breaths despite the definite pulse
Chest compressions are not indicated solely because breathing is absent when a definite pulse is present.
One breath every 30 seconds
This is insufficient ventilation for an apneic adult.
No ventilation until naloxone takes effect
Ventilatory support should not be delayed while waiting for medication response.
